# Repeated samples, limit theorems, and Monte Carlo error

A single random observation can be noisy. An average of many observations is often more stable. That simple fact powers benchmark averages, simulation, minibatch gradients, polling, randomized algorithms, and empirical research—but several different mathematical ideas hide inside it.

This unit separates them:

- a **law of large numbers** says an average approaches its target;
- a **central limit theorem** describes the approximate shape and scale of its random error;
- a **concentration inequality** gives a finite-sample ceiling on the chance of a large error;
- a **Monte Carlo standard error** estimates the remaining simulation noise;
- heavy tails and dependence explain why blindly using an iid square-root rule can be dangerously optimistic.

By the end, you should be able to derive the variance of an average, distinguish convergence concepts, standardize a sample mean, decide when a Gaussian approximation is plausible, choose and interpret a concentration bound, estimate Monte Carlo error, and repair uncertainty calculations when observations arrive in correlated clusters.

## 0. The repeated-sampling mental model

Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be observations produced by repeating an experiment. The sample mean is

$$
\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

There are three layers to keep separate:

1. The population or simulation model gives each \(X_i\) a distribution with mean \(\mu\).
2. One realized dataset gives one numerical value of \(\bar X_n\).
3. Repeating the entire dataset-generation process gives a **sampling distribution** for \(\bar X_n\).

The third layer is easy to miss. An estimator is a function of random data, so before data are observed it is itself a random variable.

**Worked example — accuracy across repeated test sets.** Suppose a fixed classifier has probability \(p=0.7\) of answering a randomly drawn benchmark item correctly. Encode correctness as \(X_i\in\{0,1\}\). A test set of 100 items produces one accuracy \(\bar X_{100}\). If we independently draw 1,000 new test sets, we obtain 1,000 different accuracies. Their histogram approximates the sampling distribution of \(\bar X_{100}\); it is not the distribution of individual correctness values.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Identify the experiment, observation, estimator, and target when estimating a model's success probability from 200 independently sampled prompts.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Describe a simulation that approximates the sampling distribution of a five-die average. Explain the two nested repetitions.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A report bootstraps rows from one fixed dataset. Explain why that resampling distribution is conceptually different from repeatedly drawing fresh datasets from the unknown population.

## 1. Why averaging reduces variance

Assume initially that \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent and identically distributed—**iid**—with

$$
E[X_i]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.
$$

Linearity of expectation gives

$$
E[\bar X_n]
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nE[X_i]
=\mu.
$$

Independence makes all cross-covariances zero, so

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\operatorname{SD}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

This is the square-root law: multiplying the sample size by four halves the standard deviation of the mean. Multiplying it by one hundred divides that standard deviation by ten.

![Several running sample means fluctuate strongly at first and then settle into a band that narrows at the inverse-square-root rate.](../assets/averaging-stabilizes.svg)

The paths in the diagram do not have to move steadily toward \(\mu\). New observations can temporarily move an average away. Stability is a statement about the shrinking distribution of error, not monotone progress along every realized path.

**Worked example — Bernoulli accuracy.** If \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.7)\), then \(\sigma^2=p(1-p)=0.21\). At \(n=100\), the standard deviation of observed accuracy across independent test sets is

$$
\sqrt{\frac{0.21}{100}}\approx0.0458.
$$

At \(n=10{,}000\), it is approximately \(0.00458\). One extra decimal place of stability costs roughly one hundred times as many independent items.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Derive the mean and variance of an average of 25 iid variables with mean 4 and variance 9.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Two independent estimates use \(n\) and \(9n\) observations. Compare their standard deviations and the widths of equally calibrated error bars.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Derive the variance of a weighted average \(\sum_iw_iX_i\) for independent observations. Under the constraint \(\sum_iw_i=1\) and equal variances, show why equal weights minimize variance.

## 2. Convergence in probability and the weak law

A sequence of random variables \(Y_n\) converges **in probability** to a constant \(c\) if, for every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\),

$$
P(|Y_n-c|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.
$$

Write this as \(Y_n\xrightarrow{P}c\).

The weak law of large numbers states, under common conditions such as iid observations with finite mean,

$$
\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu.
$$

Translate the symbols into a sentence: choose any fixed error tolerance, however small. The probability that the sample mean misses the population mean by more than that tolerance eventually becomes arbitrarily small.

The weak law does **not** say:

- \(\bar X_n=\mu\) for a finite \(n\);
- error decreases on every step of a realized run;
- all distributions converge at the same speed;
- a dataset with dependent or shifting observations behaves as if it were iid.

**Worked example — interpreting the event.** Let \(X_i\) be response latency with mean \(200\) ms. Setting \(\varepsilon=10\) ms makes the deviation event

$$
\{|\bar X_n-200|>10\}.
$$

The law says the probability of this event vanishes with \(n\); it does not supply a usable sample size by itself.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Write in words what \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu\) means for a fixed \(\varepsilon=0.01\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Give a numerical sequence of realized running means that moves away from \(\mu\) several times but still approaches it. Explain why this does not contradict convergence.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Construct random variables \(Y_n\) that equal 1 with probability \(1/n\) and 0 otherwise. Prove convergence in probability to zero and discuss whether any single realization must be eventually zero.

## 3. A weak-law proof from Chebyshev's inequality

Chebyshev's inequality says that any random variable \(Y\) with finite variance obeys

$$
P(|Y-E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)
\le
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{\varepsilon^2}.
$$

Apply it to the iid sample mean:

$$
P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)
\le
\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.
$$

For fixed \(\sigma^2\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), the right side approaches zero. This proves a finite-variance version of the weak law.

Notice the proof's architecture:

1. show the estimator is centered at the target;
2. show its variance shrinks;
3. convert shrinking variance into shrinking deviation probability.

That template reappears throughout statistics and learning theory.

**Worked example — a valid but loose guarantee.** Suppose \(\sigma^2=4\), \(n=1{,}000\), and the tolerance is \(0.2\). Chebyshev gives

$$
P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge0.2)
\le\frac{4}{1000(0.2)^2}=0.1.
$$

The true probability might be far smaller. An inequality is a guaranteed ceiling under its assumptions, not an estimate of the actual tail probability.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Use Chebyshev to bound \(P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge0.5)\) when \(\sigma^2=9\) and \(n=400\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Solve \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\le\delta\) for \(n\). Interpret the resulting sample-size requirement.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Repeat the proof for independent but non-identically distributed variables with common mean and variances bounded by \(V\). Identify the precise step where independence is used.

## 4. Almost-sure convergence and the strong law

Convergence in probability asks about the deviation probability separately at each \(n\). **Almost-sure convergence** asks about an entire infinite sample path:

$$
P\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar X_n=\mu\right)=1.
$$

Write \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu\). Under standard iid finite-mean assumptions, the strong law of large numbers gives this stronger conclusion.

A useful mental picture is:

- weak law: at a large chosen time, most paths are close;
- strong law: with probability one, a whole path eventually stays within every fixed tolerance.

“Almost surely” still allows an exceptional set of paths, but that set has probability zero. Probability zero is not the same logical statement as impossibility; a continuous variable taking one exact value is the familiar example.

We will use the strong law as a theorem rather than prove it here. Its proof requires tools beyond the finite-variance Chebyshev argument above.

> **Practice — Foundation:** State the difference between convergence in probability and almost-sure convergence without using the phrase “stronger convergence.”
>
> **Practice — Core:** Draw or describe three infinite paths where most are close at every large fixed \(n\), then explain what additional pathwise behavior almost-sure convergence requires.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Explain why a probability-one statement about an infinite sequence cannot generally be verified by observing one very long finite prefix.

## 5. Sampling distributions and standard error

The **standard error** of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. For an iid mean with known variance,

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

Usually \(\sigma\) is unknown. The sample variance

$$
s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2
$$

produces the estimated standard error

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X_n)=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
$$

Keep three quantities distinct:

- \(s\) describes spread among individual observations;
- \(s/\sqrt n\) estimates spread among repeated sample means;
- \(|\bar X_n-\mu|\) is the unknown realized error in this particular sample.

A standard error is not the realized error and does not guarantee that the target lies within one standard error.

**Worked example — seed-to-seed variation.** Five independent training runs produce evaluation scores \(0.71,0.75,0.69,0.74,0.76\). Their mean is \(0.73\). The sample standard deviation is about \(0.029\), so the estimated standard error of the five-run mean is about \(0.013\). Reporting \(0.73\pm0.029\) describes run spread; reporting a multiple of \(0.013\) addresses uncertainty in the average under an iid-run model.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Explain the difference between standard deviation and standard error for 100 observed losses.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Compute the sample standard deviation and estimated standard error for \(2,4,4,6\). Then predict how the standard error changes if the same distribution is sampled 16 times.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A paper reports a tiny standard error over one million tokens from only four independently trained models. Identify two possible observational units and explain which target each uncertainty calculation would address.

## 6. The central limit theorem

The iid central limit theorem says that if \(X_i\) have mean \(\mu\) and finite, positive variance \(\sigma^2\), then

$$
Z_n=
\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}
\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

Convergence in distribution means the CDF of \(Z_n\) approaches the standard Gaussian CDF at its continuity points.

The standardization performs three jobs:

1. subtract \(\mu\) to center the error at zero;
2. multiply by \(\sqrt n\) so the shrinking error remains visible;
3. divide by \(\sigma\) to express error in standard-deviation units.

![A skewed standardized sampling distribution becomes smoother and more Gaussian as sample size grows.](../assets/clt-shape.svg)

Undoing the standardization gives the approximation

$$
\bar X_n\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

for sufficiently large \(n\). The CLT describes the distribution of the average, not necessarily the distribution of the original \(X_i\). Highly non-Gaussian observations can still produce an approximately Gaussian mean.

If the observations themselves are Gaussian, the sample mean is exactly Gaussian for every \(n\); no approximation or large-sample argument is needed.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Standardize a sample mean of iid variables when \(n=64\), \(\mu=10\), and \(\sigma=4\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Starting from the standardized CLT, derive the approximate distribution of the sum \(S_n=\sum_iX_i\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Explain why the unscaled error \(\bar X_n-\mu\) converges to zero while the scaled error \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\) can converge to a non-degenerate distribution.

## 7. Using a Gaussian approximation carefully

Suppose \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\). Then

$$
\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N\!\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}n\right).
$$

**Worked example — unusually high observed accuracy.** Let \(p=0.72\) and \(n=200\). The standard deviation of the accuracy is

$$
\sqrt{\frac{0.72(0.28)}{200}}\approx0.03175.
$$

An observed accuracy of \(0.78\) is approximately

$$
z=\frac{0.78-0.72}{0.03175}\approx1.89
$$

standard deviations above the target. A standard Gaussian upper tail beyond \(1.89\) is about \(0.029\).

But accuracy is a discrete count divided by \(n\). The event \(\bar X_n\ge0.78\) means at least 156 successes. A continuity correction approximates this count event using boundary \(155.5\):

$$
z_{\text{cc}}
=\frac{155.5-200(0.72)}{\sqrt{200(0.72)(0.28)}}
\approx1.81.
$$

The correction respects that the continuous approximation is standing in for discrete probability bars.

Do not turn “\(n\ge30\)” into a law. Approximation quality depends on skewness, discreteness, tails, and the event being approximated. For Bernoulli sums, checking whether both \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\) are reasonably large is more informative than checking \(n\) alone.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(p=0.5,n=100\), compute the mean and standard deviation of the success count and of the observed proportion.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Approximate \(P(\bar X_n\le0.4)\) for \(p=0.5,n=100\), first without and then with a continuity correction.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Compare exact binomial and Gaussian-approximation tail probabilities over several \(p,n\) pairs. Find a case where the center is approximated well but an extreme tail is not.

## 8. When the ordinary CLT approximation fails

The theorem has assumptions, and the approximation has a regime.

- **Too little averaging:** small \(n\) can preserve skewness, gaps, and multimodality.
- **Rare events:** a large \(n\) is not enough when \(np\) remains small.
- **Extreme tails:** convergence near the center can be much better than far into a tail.
- **Infinite variance:** the usual \(\sqrt n\) scaling and Gaussian limit may fail.
- **Dependence:** correlated observations change the variance and sometimes the limit.
- **Nonstationarity:** if distributions shift with \(i\), there may be no single stable \(\mu\).
- **Selection:** stopping or reporting based on observed results changes the relevant distribution.

**Worked example — rare errors.** Let an independent request fail with probability \(p=0.002\), and observe \(n=100\) requests. Although \(n\) sounds moderately large, \(np=0.2\). The exact probability of zero failures is

$$
(1-0.002)^{100}\approx0.819.
$$

The count distribution has a large point mass at zero and strong right skew. A Gaussian approximation centered at \(0.2\) cannot represent this shape well. A Poisson approximation with rate \(0.2\) is much more natural.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For a Bernoulli sum, calculate \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\) at \(n=1{,}000,p=0.001\) and assess a Gaussian approximation.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Give one example for each failure category above and state which part of the standard CLT argument becomes doubtful.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Simulate means from a heavy-tailed distribution at growing sample sizes. Compare their sampling histograms with those from a finite-variance distribution and explain why “more data” can look erratic for a long time.

## 9. Monte Carlo estimation is expectation by sampling

Suppose a target can be written

$$
\theta=E[h(X)]
$$

but the expectation is difficult to compute analytically. Draw \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and use

$$
\hat\theta_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nh(X_i).
$$

This is Monte Carlo estimation. It is just a sample mean applied to the transformed variable \(h(X)\).

For an event \(A\), choose the indicator \(h(X)=\mathbf1\{X\in A\}\). Then

$$
\theta=P(X\in A),
\qquad
\hat\theta_n=\frac{\text{number of simulated hits}}n.
$$

If the draws are iid, the estimator is unbiased and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)
=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(h(X))}{n}.
$$

**Worked example — estimating a rare event.** To estimate \(P(S\ge25)\) for a complicated random sum \(S\), simulate \(S_i\) and average \(I_i=\mathbf1\{S_i\ge25\}\). If 48 of 100,000 simulations hit, then \(\hat p=0.00048\). The plug-in standard error is approximately

$$
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}
\approx0.000069.
$$

Only 48 effective hits support the estimate. The large total draw count should not create false confidence about a very small tail probability.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Write an indicator-based Monte Carlo estimator for \(P(g(X)>t)\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the variance of the event-probability estimator and find its worst case over \(p\in[0,1]\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a paired Monte Carlo comparison of two systems using the same random inputs. Derive why estimating the mean paired difference can have lower variance than subtracting two independent estimates.

## 10. Planning and monitoring Monte Carlo error

For iid draws with finite variance, a rough large-sample error bar is

$$
\hat\theta_n\pm z\,\frac{s_h}{\sqrt n},
$$

where \(s_h\) is the sample standard deviation of \(h(X_i)\) and \(z\) is a chosen Gaussian multiplier such as \(1.96\).

To target standard error at most \(r\), the idealized sample-size equation is

$$
n\ge\frac{\sigma_h^2}{r^2}.
$$

Because \(\sigma_h^2\) is unknown, use a pilot run or a conservative bound. For an indicator, \(p(1-p)\le1/4\), so

$$
n\ge\frac{1}{4r^2}
$$

guarantees the target standard-error scale under independent sampling. Achieving \(r=0.001\) can therefore require up to 250,000 draws.

**Stopping caution.** If you inspect estimates repeatedly and stop precisely when an ordinary interval first excludes an inconvenient value, its nominal coverage no longer applies automatically. A fixed sample size, a predeclared precision rule with appropriate sequential analysis, or an untouched confirmation run makes the inferential target clearer.

Also separate Monte Carlo error from model error. A billion flawless simulations can estimate the wrong probability extremely precisely if the simulator is misspecified.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Under the worst-case Bernoulli variance, calculate the sample size needed for standard error at most \(0.005\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** A pilot run estimates \(\sigma_h=12\). Determine the approximate draw count required to halve the current standard error.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a simulation report that separates random-number seed, Monte Carlo standard error, numerical error, and simulator misspecification.

## 11. Concentration inequalities give finite-sample ceilings

Limit theorems describe behavior as \(n\) grows. Concentration inequalities provide statements valid at a particular finite \(n\).

**Markov's inequality.** For nonnegative \(Y\) and \(a>0\),

$$
P(Y\ge a)\le\frac{E[Y]}a.
$$

The proof is one line: \(Y\ge a\mathbf1\{Y\ge a\}\); take expectations.

**Chebyshev's inequality.** Apply Markov to \((Y-E[Y])^2\):

$$
P(|Y-E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)
\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{\varepsilon^2}.
$$

**Hoeffding's inequality.** If independent observations satisfy \(X_i\in[a,b]\), then

$$
P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)
\le
2\exp\!\left(
-\frac{2n\varepsilon^2}{(b-a)^2}
\right).
$$

Stronger assumptions buy a faster, exponential tail ceiling.

![Markov, Chebyshev, and Hoeffding use progressively stronger assumptions to control increasingly sharp tail regions.](../assets/concentration-assumptions.svg)

**Worked comparison.** For independent \(X_i\in[0,1]\), \(n=500\), and \(\varepsilon=0.1\), the worst-case variance is \(1/4\). Chebyshev gives

$$
\frac{1/4}{500(0.1)^2}=0.05,
$$

while Hoeffding gives

$$
2e^{-2(500)(0.1)^2}
=2e^{-10}\approx0.0000908.
$$

Neither is automatically close to the true tail probability. Choose a bound by checking its assumptions, not by selecting the smallest number after the fact.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Use Markov to bound \(P(Y\ge20)\) for nonnegative \(Y\) with mean 3.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive Chebyshev from Markov, then apply Hoeffding to a mean of 800 independent values in \([-1,1]\) with tolerance \(0.1\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Find a regime where the numerical Chebyshev bound is smaller than the Hoeffding bound even though Hoeffding has exponential decay. Explain why “asymptotically sharper” need not mean smaller for every parameter choice.

## 12. Heavy tails and robust summaries

A heavy-tailed distribution places non-negligible probability far from its center. The practical issue is not merely that outliers look dramatic: the moments required by familiar guarantees may not exist.

For a Pareto-type tail with parameter \(\alpha\):

- when \(\alpha\le1\), the mean is infinite;
- when \(1<\alpha\le2\), the mean exists but variance is infinite;
- when \(\alpha>2\), both mean and variance exist, though convergence can still be slow when \(\alpha\) is near 2.

If variance is infinite, the ordinary variance calculation for \(\bar X_n\), the \(s/\sqrt n\) standard error, Chebyshev's inequality, and the ordinary finite-variance CLT are not justified.

**Worked example — one observation dominates.** The nine values

$$
2,3,3,4,4,4,5,5,970
$$

have mean \(111.1\) but median \(4\). Neither summary is universally “correct”: the mean answers total divided by count and is appropriate for some cost targets, while the median describes a typical observation. The point is to choose a target and an estimator whose sensitivity matches the decision.

Robust options include:

- median or quantiles when the target is typical behavior;
- trimmed or winsorized means when a bounded influence rule is scientifically defensible;
- median-of-means: split observations into groups, average within each group, then take the median of group means;
- an explicit heavy-tailed model when tail behavior itself is the target.

Never delete extreme observations solely because they are inconvenient. First distinguish data errors, rare valid events, and a misspecified model.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compare the mean and median before and after adding one extreme value to a small dataset.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Implement median-of-means for 100 values using ten groups. Explain how group count trades robustness against the stability of each group mean.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Construct a decision problem where the mean is essential despite heavy tails and another where a high quantile is the more relevant target. Justify both choices.

## 13. Dependence changes the effective sample size

For observations with common variance \(\sigma^2\) but possible dependence,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)
=\frac1{n^2}
\left[
n\sigma^2
+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)
\right].
$$

Positive covariance inflates uncertainty. Negative covariance can reduce it. The iid formula silently discards every covariance term.

For a weakly stationary sequence with lag-\(k\) autocorrelation \(\rho_k\), a large-\(n\) approximation is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)
\approx
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k\right).
$$

Define an approximate effective sample size

$$
n_{\text{eff}}
\approx
\frac{n}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}.
$$

It is the iid sample size that would give roughly the same mean variance. It is a summary under assumptions, not a count of magically independent rows.

![Twenty-four weakly dependent observations carry more independent information than twenty-four observations arranged in a few repeated blocks.](../assets/dependence-effective-sample.svg)

**Worked example — persistent sequence.** If correlations resemble \(\rho_k=\rho^k\) with \(\rho=0.8\), then

$$
1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho^k
=1+\frac{2\rho}{1-\rho}
=9.
$$

Thus \(n_{\text{eff}}\approx n/9\). Nine thousand sequential measurements may provide uncertainty similar to only about one thousand iid measurements.

For clustered data, resample or aggregate at the independent unit: user, conversation, task, document, environment, or training run. For time series and Markov-chain output, methods include autocorrelation-aware estimators and **batch means**: divide a sufficiently long sequence into contiguous batches, average within each, and estimate uncertainty from variation among batch averages.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Identify the likely independent unit for tokens within responses, responses within users, and seeds within one training configuration.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the variance of the mean when every distinct pair has covariance \(c\). Describe what happens when \(c>0\) stays fixed as \(n\) grows.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Simulate an autocorrelated sequence, compare the iid standard error with a batch-means estimate, and study sensitivity to batch length and number of batches.

## 14. Research and ML evaluation patterns

Repeated-sample reasoning appears throughout AI work:

- **Benchmark accuracy:** rows may share templates, authors, tasks, or contamination sources.
- **LLM judging:** repeated judge calls share prompts and model biases; judge randomness is only one uncertainty source.
- **Training curves:** adjacent checkpoints and minibatches are strongly dependent.
- **Multiple seeds:** seeds sample optimization randomness but not necessarily datasets, architectures, or research choices.
- **Agent rollouts:** turns within an episode share state; episode-level outcomes are often the safer unit.
- **Token losses:** millions of tokens can come from a small number of documents, so token count overstates independent information.
- **A/B evaluation:** paired prompts make the within-prompt difference the natural estimator and can remove prompt difficulty variation.
- **Simulation:** Monte Carlo precision does not validate the simulator, reward, policy, or deployment distribution.

**Worked example — paired model comparison.** On prompt \(i\), let \(A_i,B_i\in\{0,1\}\) be correctness for two models and define \(D_i=A_i-B_i\). Estimate the performance difference by \(\bar D\). Its variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(D_i)
=\operatorname{Var}(A_i)+\operatorname{Var}(B_i)
-2\operatorname{Cov}(A_i,B_i).
$$

If both models tend to succeed on easy prompts and fail on hard ones, covariance is positive, so pairing reduces variance relative to two independent prompt sets. The independent unit still may be a task family rather than an individual prompt.

Before attaching an error bar, answer:

1. What randomness is the probability statement over?
2. What is the target population or simulator?
3. Which units are plausibly independent?
4. Is the estimator's variance finite and stable?
5. Were stopping, filtering, or model selection decisions data-dependent?

> **Practice — Foundation:** For each ML example above, name the estimator, target, and plausible independent unit.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Redesign an evaluation with 5,000 prompts nested in 100 tasks so that uncertainty reflects task-to-task variation rather than treating all rows as iid.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Write an uncertainty audit for a best-of-20-seeds result. Separate within-seed evaluation noise, seed variation, selection bias, and uncertainty about transfer to a new dataset.

## 15. Runnable lab: batch-means standard error

Implement **batch_means_standard_error** in [labs/exercises.py](../../labs/exercises.py). Given a finite numeric sequence and a positive batch size that divides its length into at least two batches, return:

1. the overall sample mean;
2. the standard error estimated from the sample variance of contiguous batch means.

Run:

~~~text
python -m labs.checks monte-carlo
~~~

The checks cover batch size one, constant data, translation and scale behavior, large offsets, input preservation, and invalid batch layouts.

### Guided experiment

Generate three sequences with the same marginal mean and variance:

1. iid Gaussian observations;
2. a positively autocorrelated sequence;
3. a sequence formed by repeating every iid draw several times.

For several batch sizes, compare the naive iid standard error with the batch-means estimate. Repeat the entire experiment to learn which batch sizes are too short to absorb dependence and which leave too few batches for stable variance estimation.

## 16. Derivations to own

1. Derive the mean and variance of an iid sample mean.
2. Prove the finite-variance weak law using Chebyshev.
3. Convert the standardized CLT into approximations for a mean and a sum.
4. Derive the Bernoulli mean standard error.
5. Derive Monte Carlo variance for a transformed variable and for an indicator.
6. Prove Markov's inequality and derive Chebyshev from it.
7. Compare the \(1/n\) Chebyshev ceiling with exponential Hoeffding decay.
8. Expand the variance of a dependent sample mean into covariance terms.
9. Derive the effective-sample-size expression from autocorrelations.
10. Derive the variance of a paired estimator and state when pairing helps.

## 17. End-of-unit practice (graded)

**Foundation — problems 1–4.** Read sampling distributions and execute direct variance and approximation calculations.

1. **Average mechanics.** Let iid observations have mean 12 and variance 25. Find the mean, variance, and standard error of \(\bar X_{100}\). Recompute for \(\bar X_{400}\).
2. **Convergence language.** Translate the weak law and strong law into plain language, then give one claim neither law makes about a finite sample.
3. **Bernoulli sampling.** For \(p=0.4,n=250\), compute the mean and standard deviation of the success count and the sample proportion.
4. **Markov and Chebyshev.** Bound a nonnegative tail using Markov, then bound a centered deviation using Chebyshev for numerical values of your choice.

**Core — problems 5–9.** Combine theorems, choose approximations, and quantify Monte Carlo error.

5. **Weak-law proof.** Prove convergence in probability for independent variables sharing mean \(\mu\) whose variances are all at most \(V\).
6. **Continuity correction.** Approximate \(P(S\ge65)\) for \(S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,0.5)\) with and without a continuity correction; compare with an exact computation.
7. **Monte Carlo planning.** Derive a conservative draw count for estimating any Bernoulli probability with approximate 95% half-width at most \(0.002\).
8. **Concentration choice.** For independent losses in \([0,4]\), compare Chebyshev and Hoeffding bounds for a specified \(n,\varepsilon\). List the assumptions used by each.
9. **Paired evaluation.** Given paired binary predictions from two models, compute the mean difference, its estimated standard error, and the result obtained after incorrectly treating model scores as independent.

**Stretch — problems 10–14.** Audit broken assumptions and design defensible repeated-sample evidence.

10. **Rare events.** Compare exact binomial, Poisson, Gaussian, and Hoeffding calculations for at least one rare-event setting. Explain which numbers are approximations, exact probabilities, or guaranteed ceilings.
11. **Heavy tails.** Simulate a finite-mean, infinite-variance distribution. Compare sample mean, trimmed mean, median, and median-of-means across increasing sample sizes and repeated datasets.
12. **Dependence.** Generate sequences with several autocorrelation strengths. Compare empirical variance across repeated sequence means with iid and batch-means standard-error predictions.
13. **Hierarchical benchmark.** Design an estimator and uncertainty procedure for prompts nested within tasks, tasks nested within domains, and multiple stochastic model runs. State the population to which each conclusion generalizes.
14. **Research critique.** Find or invent a result that reports a mean over a huge row count but has few independent units. Reconstruct a plausible dependence structure, estimate how uncertainty changes, and rewrite the claim conservatively.

<details><summary>Worked solution sketches</summary>

1. The mean remains 12. Variance is \(25/n\), giving \(0.25\) and \(0.0625\); standard errors are \(0.5\) and \(0.25\). Four times the data halves the standard error.
2. The weak law makes fixed-\(n\) deviation probabilities vanish; the strong law says almost every infinite running-average path converges. Neither guarantees exact equality, monotone error reduction, or a useful finite-\(n\) rate.
3. The count has mean \(100\) and variance \(60\), hence standard deviation \(\sqrt{60}\). The proportion has mean \(0.4\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.4(0.6)/250}\).
4. Markov gives \(P(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]/a\) for nonnegative \(Y\). Chebyshev gives \(P(|Y-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\). A complete answer verifies positivity of thresholds and finite moments.
5. The average has expectation \(\mu\) and variance at most \(V/n\) because independence removes covariance terms. Chebyshev bounds the deviation probability by \(V/(n\varepsilon^2)\), which vanishes.
6. The uncorrected standardized boundary is \((65-50)/5=3\); the corrected one uses \(64.5\), giving \(2.9\). Exact binomial summation determines which approximation is closer.
7. With multiplier \(1.96\) and worst-case variance \(1/4\), require \(1.96\sqrt{1/(4n)}\le0.002\), or \(n\ge1.96^2/(4\cdot0.002^2)\), approximately 240,100 independent draws.
8. Chebyshev uses finite variance; bound it by the range if necessary. Hoeffding uses independence and boundedness and substitutes range width \(4\). Report both ceilings even if either exceeds one, then truncate a probability ceiling at one.
9. Form differences \(D_i=A_i-B_i\) and use their sample standard deviation divided by \(\sqrt n\). Ignoring pairing omits the covariance term and is usually less precise when prompt difficulty affects both models similarly.
10. Exact binomial summation is the reference under iid Bernoulli assumptions. Poisson and Gaussian values approximate it under different regimes. Hoeffding is a finite-sample upper bound and need not approximate the true probability.
11. Results depend on the tail parameter and tuning choices. The ordinary mean targets the expectation but can be dominated by extremes; robust summaries stabilize different targets or trade bias for reduced sensitivity. Report repeated-sample distributions, not one favorable run.
12. Positive autocorrelation inflates empirical variance above \(\sigma^2/n\). Batch means improve only when batches are long enough relative to dependence and numerous enough to estimate between-batch variance reliably.
13. A defensible design names whether domains and tasks are fixed or sampled, aggregates or resamples at the intended generalization unit, preserves run and prompt pairing, and reports variance components rather than one row-level iid interval.
14. Replacing row count by independent cluster count usually widens uncertainty. The revised claim should name the observed clusters, avoid unsupported population generalization, and distinguish descriptive precision from evidence across genuinely new units.

</details>

## Mastery check

Given a repeated-sampling problem, identify the target, estimator, and independent unit; derive the estimator's mean and variance; state whether an LLN, CLT, or concentration result applies; quantify Monte Carlo error; and diagnose heavy-tail, dependence, stopping, or selection failures. Validate at least one analytic prediction with repeated simulation rather than one long run.

# Estimation, likelihood, Fisher information, and asymptotics

Probability starts with a model and derives what data might look like. Estimation reverses the direction: data have been observed, but some feature of the model or population is unknown.

That reversal creates several distinct questions:

- What quantity are we trying to learn?
- Which function of the data will estimate it?
- Across repeated datasets, is that function systematically wrong or highly variable?
- How does a probabilistic model turn observed data into a likelihood?
- When does maximizing likelihood recover the target?
- How much information does one observation carry?
- When are Gaussian standard-error calculations justified?

This chapter builds those ideas from finite examples to the asymptotic tools used in research. By the end, you should be able to distinguish a parameter from an estimator and an estimate, derive bias–variance–MSE decompositions, obtain Bernoulli and Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimators, diagnose non-identifiability, calculate Fisher information, explain consistency and asymptotic normality, use the delta method, and identify where misspecification or dependence invalidates familiar uncertainty formulas.

## 0. Parameter, estimand, estimator, and estimate

Suppose data \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) come from an unknown distribution \(P\).

- A **parameter** is a coordinate in a model, such as the Bernoulli probability \(p\).
- An **estimand** is the population quantity we choose to learn, such as \(E_P[X]\), a median, or an accuracy difference. It need not be a model parameter.
- An **estimator** is a rule applied to random data:

$$
\hat\theta=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n).
$$

- An **estimate** is the numerical value of that rule after one dataset is observed.

The hat marks a random estimator before observation and a realized estimate after observation; context tells which meaning is intended.

**Worked example — estimating correctness.** Let \(X_i=1\) if a model answers prompt \(i\) correctly and \(0\) otherwise. Under an iid Bernoulli model, \(p\) is the unknown success probability, \(\hat p=\frac1n\sum_iX_i\) is an estimator, and \(0.73\) might be its value on one test set. If the target population changes from public benchmarks to deployed user requests, the estimand changes even if the formula for \(\hat p\) does not.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Label the parameter, estimator, estimate, and data in a study that reports an average latency of 182 ms from 500 requests.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Give an estimand that is not naturally a finite-dimensional model parameter, and construct an estimator for it.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Describe two different target populations for the same model-evaluation dataset. Explain why the same numerical estimate need not support both generalizations.

## 1. An estimator has a sampling distribution

Before data are observed, \(\hat\theta\) varies from dataset to dataset. Its probability law under a fixed data-generating distribution is the estimator's **sampling distribution**.

To study it conceptually:

1. fix the population or model parameter \(\theta\);
2. draw a complete dataset of size \(n\);
3. compute \(\hat\theta\);
4. repeat steps 2–3 many times.

This repeated-dataset thought experiment defines quantities such as

$$
E_\theta[\hat\theta],
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta),
\qquad
P_\theta(|\hat\theta-\theta|>\varepsilon).
$$

The subscript reminds us that estimator behavior can depend on the unknown truth. An estimator can be excellent at one parameter value and poor at another.

**Worked example — two estimators of a mean.** For iid data with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), both \(X_1\) and \(\bar X_n\) are unbiased estimators of \(\mu\). Their variances are \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma^2/n\). Unbiasedness alone does not distinguish them, but their sampling distributions do.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Describe how to simulate the sampling distribution of a sample median from a known distribution.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Compare \(X_1\) and \((X_1+X_2)/2\) as estimators of a common mean, including expectation and variance.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Construct an estimator whose sampling distribution depends strongly on \(\theta\), then identify a parameter region where it performs poorly.

## 2. Bias and variance measure different errors

The bias of an estimator at \(\theta\) is

$$
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(\hat\theta)
=E_\theta[\hat\theta]-\theta.
$$

An estimator is **unbiased** if this equals zero for every permitted \(\theta\). Its variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)
=E_\theta\!\left[
(\hat\theta-E_\theta[\hat\theta])^2
\right].
$$

Bias measures displacement of the sampling-distribution center from the target. Variance measures spread around that center.

![Sampling distributions can be centered but wide, shifted but narrow, or both centered and narrow.](../assets/estimator-bias-variance.svg)

An unbiased estimator can be too noisy to use. A mildly biased estimator can make smaller errors overall. Bias is not automatically a defect; hidden or unquantified bias is the danger.

**Worked example — a deliberately biased mean.** If \(\bar X_n\) estimates \(\mu\), define

$$
\tilde\mu=\frac{n}{n+1}\bar X_n.
$$

Then

$$
E[\tilde\mu]=\frac{n}{n+1}\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Bias}(\tilde\mu)=-\frac{\mu}{n+1},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\mu)
=\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^2\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

The shrinkage introduces bias but lowers variance. Whether it helps depends on \(\mu,\sigma^2\), and the loss used to judge error.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the bias of \(2\bar X_n\) as an estimator of \(\mu\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Find the bias and variance of \(a\bar X_n+b\) for estimating \(\mu\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Give an example where unbiasedness is a poor primary design criterion because rare, enormous errors dominate the estimator's usefulness.

## 3. Mean squared error combines bias and variance

Under squared-error loss, the mean squared error is

$$
\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(\hat\theta)
=E_\theta[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2].
$$

Add and subtract \(E[\hat\theta]\):

$$
\hat\theta-\theta
=
(\hat\theta-E[\hat\theta])
+
(E[\hat\theta]-\theta).
$$

After squaring and taking expectations, the cross-term vanishes because \(E[\hat\theta-E[\hat\theta]]=0\). Therefore

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(\hat\theta)
=
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)
+
\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(\hat\theta)^2
}.
$$

This identity is about one estimator at one parameter value. Comparing estimators globally requires specifying whether we care about worst-case MSE, average MSE under a distribution of parameter values, or performance in a particular region.

**Worked example — when shrinkage helps.** For \(\tilde\mu=a\bar X_n\),

$$
\operatorname{MSE}(\tilde\mu)
=a^2\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+(a-1)^2\mu^2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to \(a\) gives the MSE-minimizing value

$$
a^*=\frac{\mu^2}{\mu^2+\sigma^2/n}.
$$

This oracle value depends on unknown \(\mu\), so it is not directly usable. The calculation still reveals why stronger shrinkage is attractive when sampling noise is large relative to signal.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute MSE from bias \(0.2\) and variance \(0.09\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the bias–variance decomposition without skipping the cross-term.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Compare two estimators whose MSE curves cross as \(\theta\) changes. Explain why declaring one estimator “best” requires a parameter region or decision criterion.

## 4. The plug-in principle and empirical distribution

Many estimators arise by replacing an unknown population distribution with the empirical distribution, which assigns mass \(1/n\) to each observation.

If

$$
\theta=E_P[g(X)],
$$

the plug-in estimator is

$$
\hat\theta
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ng(X_i).
$$

Examples include:

- population mean \(\rightarrow\) sample mean;
- event probability \(\rightarrow\) observed event fraction;
- population second moment \(\rightarrow n^{-1}\sum_iX_i^2\);
- population CDF \(F(t)\) \(\rightarrow n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf1\{X_i\le t\}\).

Plug-in does not guarantee unbiasedness. The population variance can be written

$$
\sigma^2=E[(X-\mu)^2].
$$

Replacing both \(P\) and \(\mu\) gives

$$
\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2,
$$

which is biased downward for iid finite-variance data because the same observations estimated the center. Multiplying by \(n/(n-1)\) gives the familiar unbiased sample variance when \(n\ge2\).

> **Practice — Foundation:** Write plug-in estimators for \(E[X^3]\) and \(P(X>5)\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show algebraically that \(n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i^2-\bar X^2\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Find a nonlinear population functional for which a naive plug-in estimate is biased. Use simulation to study whether the bias vanishes with sample size.

## 5. Likelihood compares parameter values after data are fixed

Let a model assign density or mass \(p_\theta(x)\) to observation \(x\). For iid observed data \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the likelihood is

$$
L(\theta;x_{1:n})
=\prod_{i=1}^np_\theta(x_i).
$$

The same expression is read in two directions:

- as a function of possible data with \(\theta\) fixed, it is a probability mass or density;
- as a function of \(\theta\) with observed data fixed, it is a likelihood.

A likelihood need not integrate or sum to one over \(\theta\). It is not a posterior probability distribution over parameters.

Products of many probabilities underflow, so use the log-likelihood

$$
\ell(\theta)
=\log L(\theta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(x_i).
$$

The logarithm preserves the maximizer because it is strictly increasing.

![With data fixed, a larger sample usually produces a sharper log-likelihood peak around its maximizer.](../assets/likelihood-curvature.svg)

Likelihood is comparative within a specified model. A high likelihood under one parameter does not prove the model family is adequate, and raw likelihoods from datasets of different sizes are not directly comparable.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Explain why \(L(\theta;x)\) is not generally a probability distribution over \(\theta\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the log-likelihood for iid Poisson observations and identify which data summary it depends on.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Construct two model families whose likelihood maxima cannot be compared meaningfully without accounting for model complexity or predictive evaluation.

## 6. Bernoulli maximum likelihood from first principles

For observations \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) and success count \(s=\sum_ix_i\),

$$
L(p)=p^s(1-p)^{n-s},
\qquad 0\le p\le1.
$$

For \(0<p<1\),

$$
\ell(p)=s\log p+(n-s)\log(1-p).
$$

Differentiate:

$$
\ell'(p)=\frac{s}{p}-\frac{n-s}{1-p}.
$$

Setting the score to zero gives

$$
s(1-p)=(n-s)p
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat p_{\text{MLE}}=\frac{s}{n}.
$$

The second derivative

$$
\ell''(p)
=-\frac{s}{p^2}-\frac{n-s}{(1-p)^2}
$$

is negative in the interior, confirming a maximum.

**Boundary cases matter.** If \(s=0\), the maximum is \(p=0\); if \(s=n\), it is \(p=1\). The derivative-zero argument does not find these boundary maxima.

**Worked example — seven successes.** For \(s=7,n=10\), the MLE is \(0.7\), and the maximized log-likelihood is

$$
7\log(0.7)+3\log(0.3)\approx-6.109.
$$

This negative number is normal: probabilities are at most one, so their logarithms are nonpositive.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Derive the Bernoulli MLE for 18 successes in 30 trials and evaluate the score at the answer.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Compare the likelihood at \(p=0.4,0.6,0.8\) for 8 successes in 10 trials without multiplying tiny numbers.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Study the all-success case. Explain why the plug-in Fisher standard error becomes zero and why that does not mean the unknown probability is known exactly.

## 7. General maximum-likelihood workflow

A maximum-likelihood estimator is

$$
\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}
\in\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell(\theta).
$$

The notation permits multiple maximizers. A reliable workflow is:

1. specify the observation model and parameter space \(\Theta\);
2. write the joint likelihood, including dependence if present;
3. move to log space;
4. identify data terms that do not depend on \(\theta\);
5. differentiate only where valid;
6. check stationary points, boundaries, constraints, and non-identifiability;
7. verify the candidate numerically;
8. assess model fit separately from optimization success.

The equation \(\nabla\ell(\theta)=0\) is neither necessary nor sufficient for a global maximum. Constrained optima can lie on boundaries; non-concave likelihoods can have local maxima and saddle points.

**Invariance of the MLE.** If \(\eta=g(\theta)\) and \(g\) is one-to-one, then the MLE of \(\eta\) is \(g(\hat\theta)\). For many-to-one transformations, define the induced likelihood carefully and maximize over all preimages.

> **Practice — Foundation:** List the checks required after solving a score equation.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Find the MLE of the rate \(\lambda\) from iid exponential observations, including the parameter constraint.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Give a likelihood with multiple local maxima and describe how you would separate an optimization failure from genuine non-identifiability.

## 8. Gaussian MLE and the degrees-of-freedom correction

Let \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) iid with both parameters unknown. Ignoring constants,

$$
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)
=-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2.
$$

For fixed \(\sigma^2\), maximizing over \(\mu\) minimizes squared deviations, giving

$$
\hat\mu_{\text{MLE}}=\bar x.
$$

Substituting \(\bar x\) and differentiating with respect to \(\sigma^2\) gives

$$
\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2.
$$

Under iid Gaussian sampling—and more generally for iid data with finite variance—

$$
E[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}]
=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2.
$$

Thus the MLE is biased downward. The unbiased estimator is

$$
s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2.
$$

MLE and unbiasedness optimize different criteria. The MLE chooses the parameter that maximizes observed-data likelihood; the correction chooses a scaling with exact repeated-sample expectation \(\sigma^2\).

**Worked example — two observations.** For data \(0,2\), \(\bar x=1\). Squared deviations sum to 2, so the Gaussian MLE variance is \(1\), while the unbiased sample variance is \(2\). With so little data, estimating the mean has consumed substantial information about spread.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute Gaussian mean and variance MLEs for \(1,2,6\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Prove \(\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+n(\bar x-\mu)^2\) and use it to establish the mean MLE.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Simulate Gaussian samples at several \(n\) and compare empirical bias and MSE of the \(1/n\) and \(1/(n-1)\) variance estimators.

## 9. Identifiability and sufficient summaries

### Identifiability

A parameter is identifiable if different parameter values imply different observable distributions:

$$
P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta_1=\theta_2.
$$

If \(X\sim\mathcal N(\theta^2,1)\) with \(\theta\in\mathbb R\), then \(\theta\) and \(-\theta\) produce the same distribution. No amount of data can determine the sign without another assumption. This is not an optimizer defect; it is missing information in the model.

Neural networks often have parameter symmetries. Permuting hidden units can leave the represented function unchanged. Parameter non-identifiability need not prevent accurate prediction, but it changes how parameter uncertainty should be interpreted.

### Sufficiency

A statistic \(T(X)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) when, under the model, the remaining details of the sample contain no additional information about \(\theta\).

For Bernoulli data,

$$
L(p;x_{1:n})=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum x_i}.
$$

The likelihood depends on the sequence only through \(S=\sum_iX_i\), so the success count is sufficient for \(p\). Order can be discarded for estimating \(p\) under the iid Bernoulli model.

Sufficiency is model-dependent. If success probability drifts over time, order may be crucial.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Show why \(\theta\) is not identifiable in the model \(X\sim\mathcal N(\theta^2,1)\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Identify a sufficient statistic for the Poisson rate from iid observations by factoring the likelihood.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Give an example where compressing data to a formerly sufficient statistic destroys evidence after the model is expanded.

## 10. Score and Fisher information

For one observation, the **score** is the derivative of log probability or density:

$$
U_\theta(X)
=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(X).
$$

Under regularity conditions that allow differentiation through the integral,

$$
E_\theta[U_\theta(X)]=0.
$$

Fisher information can then be written in two equivalent ways:

$$
I_1(\theta)
=E_\theta[U_\theta(X)^2]
=-E_\theta\!\left[
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p_\theta(X)
\right].
$$

Interpretations:

- the score measures how one observation locally pushes the fitted parameter;
- large score variance means observations respond strongly to parameter changes;
- large negative expected curvature means the likelihood peak is locally sharp.

For independent observations, scores add and information adds:

$$
I_n(\theta)=nI_1(\theta).
$$

**Worked example — Bernoulli information.** The one-observation score is

$$
U_p(X)=\frac{X}{p}-\frac{1-X}{1-p}
=\frac{X-p}{p(1-p)}.
$$

Since \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)\),

$$
I_1(p)=\frac1{p(1-p)}.
$$

This grows near the boundary in the \(p\) parameterization, but regular asymptotic approximations become delicate there. Information is local and parameterization-dependent; it is not a universal count of useful examples.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Derive the score for one Gaussian observation when variance is known and mean is the parameter.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Compute Fisher information for the Gaussian mean and verify additivity across \(n\) independent observations.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Reparameterize Bernoulli probability by log odds \(\eta=\log(p/(1-p))\). Derive information for \(\eta\) and explain why its numerical value differs from information for \(p\).

## 11. The Cramér–Rao lower bound and efficiency

Under regularity conditions, any unbiased estimator \(\hat\theta\) satisfies

$$
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\hat\theta)
\ge
\frac1{I_n(\theta)}.
$$

This is the Cramér–Rao lower bound. It says that within the class of unbiased estimators and under the stated model, information limits precision.

For iid Bernoulli data,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)
=\frac{p(1-p)}n
=\frac1{I_n(p)}.
$$

The sample proportion attains the bound and is efficient in this finite-sample sense.

Important qualifications:

- biased estimators require a modified bound;
- boundary parameters and parameter-dependent support can violate regularity;
- nuisance parameters change the relevant information calculation;
- a lower bound inside a wrong model does not guarantee real-world accuracy;
- attaining the bound does not make the chosen estimand scientifically useful.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Evaluate the Bernoulli Cramér–Rao bound at \(p=0.5,n=100\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show that the sample mean attains the bound when estimating a Gaussian mean with known variance.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Explain how a biased shrinkage estimator can have MSE below an unbiased Cramér–Rao variance bound without contradiction.

## 12. Consistency asks whether error vanishes

An estimator is consistent for \(\theta\) if

$$
\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{P}\theta.
$$

The Bernoulli MLE \(\hat p=\bar X_n\) is consistent by the law of large numbers.

Unbiasedness and consistency are different:

- \(X_1\) is unbiased for a common mean but not consistent because it does not use increasing information;
- \(\frac{n}{n+1}\bar X_n\) is biased for every finite \(n\) but consistent because its bias and variance both vanish.

For MLE, divide the log-likelihood by \(n\):

$$
\frac1n\ell_n(\theta)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i).
$$

The law of large numbers suggests convergence to

$$
E_{\theta_0}[\log p_\theta(X)].
$$

Under identifiability and additional uniformity conditions, this expected log-likelihood is uniquely maximized at the true parameter \(\theta_0\), leading the empirical maximizer toward \(\theta_0\).

Pointwise convergence of the objective is not by itself enough to guarantee convergence of its maximizer. The parameter space, continuity, tails, and control over all candidate parameters matter.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Decide whether \(X_1\), \(\bar X_n+1/n\), and \(2\bar X_n\) are consistent for \(\mu\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Prove consistency of the sample proportion using either the weak law or Chebyshev.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Construct objective functions that converge pointwise but whose maximizers escape. Explain why MLE consistency needs more than pointwise convergence.

## 13. Asymptotic normality explains the local error shape

Under regularity conditions, a one-dimensional MLE often satisfies

$$
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac1{I_1(\theta_0)}\right).
$$

Equivalently, for large \(n\),

$$
\hat\theta
\approx
\mathcal N\!\left(
\theta_0,\frac1{nI_1(\theta_0)}
\right).
$$

![Consistency makes the raw sampling distribution contract, while asymptotic normality describes the stable shape of the square-root-scaled error.](../assets/asymptotic-estimator.svg)

The core derivation is a Taylor expansion of the sample score around the truth:

$$
0=U_n(\hat\theta)
\approx
U_n(\theta_0)
+
(\hat\theta-\theta_0)U_n'(\theta_0).
$$

Rearranging,

$$
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\approx
-
\frac{U_n(\theta_0)/\sqrt n}
{U_n'(\theta_0)/n}.
$$

The numerator follows a CLT because it is a sum of mean-zero scores. The denominator follows a law of large numbers toward \(-I_1(\theta_0)\).

In practice, substitute the estimate:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)
\approx
\frac1{\sqrt{nI_1(\hat\theta)}}.
$$

Observed information uses the realized negative Hessian; expected information averages that curvature under the model. They are asymptotically related but need not match exactly in a finite dataset.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Use Bernoulli Fisher information to recover the large-sample standard error of \(\hat p\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Fill in the Taylor-score derivation and state which limit theorem justifies numerator and denominator.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** List three nonregular settings—such as a boundary or mixture model—where the usual square-root-\(n\) Gaussian approximation can fail, and predict the failure mode.

## 14. Transforming estimators: invariance and the delta method

Often the target is \(\eta=g(\theta)\). MLE invariance suggests

$$
\hat\eta=g(\hat\theta).
$$

To approximate its uncertainty, expand \(g\) around \(\theta\):

$$
g(\hat\theta)
\approx
g(\theta)+g'(\theta)(\hat\theta-\theta).
$$

If

$$
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)
\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,V),
$$

then the delta method gives

$$
\sqrt n\bigl(g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta)\bigr)
\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal N\!\left(0,[g'(\theta)]^2V\right).
$$

For vector parameters, replace \(g'\) with the gradient or Jacobian.

**Worked example — log odds.** For Bernoulli \(p\), let

$$
g(p)=\log\frac{p}{1-p},
\qquad
g'(p)=\frac1{p(1-p)}.
$$

Since \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)\approx p(1-p)/n\),

$$
\operatorname{Var}(g(\hat p))
\approx\frac1{np(1-p)}.
$$

At \(\hat p=0.7,n=400\), the plug-in standard error on the log-odds scale is about

$$
\sqrt{\frac1{400(0.7)(0.3)}}\approx0.109.
$$

If \(g'(\theta)=0\), the first-order delta method degenerates and a higher-order expansion may be needed.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Use the delta method for \(g(\mu)=\mu^2\) when \(\bar X_n\) estimates a nonzero mean.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive an approximate variance for \(\log\hat\lambda\) when \(\hat\lambda\) is an asymptotically normal positive rate estimate.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Analyze what happens to the first-order delta method for \(g(\theta)=\theta^2\) at \(\theta=0\). Use a second-order argument to predict a non-Gaussian limit.

## 15. Regularization, penalized likelihood, and MAP

Pure maximum likelihood optimizes

$$
\ell(\theta).
$$

Penalized likelihood optimizes

$$
\ell(\theta)-\lambda R(\theta),
$$

where \(R\) encodes a preference such as small norm or smoothness. The penalty typically introduces bias while reducing variance or preventing unstable solutions.

Scaling matters. If \(\ell\) is a sum over \(n\) observations while \(\lambda\) is fixed, the data term grows with \(n\). If software minimizes average negative log-likelihood plus \(\lambda R\), the meaning of the same numerical \(\lambda\) differs.

With a prior density \(\pi(\theta)\), a maximum a posteriori estimate maximizes

$$
\ell(\theta)+\log\pi(\theta).
$$

This looks like penalized likelihood, but the interpretation differs: MAP is a posterior mode under a specified prior and parameterization.

**Worked example — Beta–Bernoulli shrinkage.** With a \(\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) prior and \(s\) successes,

$$
\hat p_{\text{MAP}}
=\frac{s+\alpha-1}{n+\alpha+\beta-2}
$$

for an interior mode when \(\alpha,\beta>1\). The posterior mean is

$$
\frac{s+\alpha}{n+\alpha+\beta}.
$$

They are different estimators. Both shrink the raw proportion toward a prior-dependent center.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Identify the likelihood term and penalty in ridge regression.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the interior Beta–Bernoulli MAP estimate and compare it with the MLE and posterior mean.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Show how changing from summed to averaged loss changes the effective regularization strength unless \(\lambda\) is rescaled.

## 16. Misspecification, dependence, and selection

The clean formulas above describe behavior under a chosen model. Real failures often come from outside its parameter coordinates.

### Misspecification

If the true distribution is not in \(\{P_\theta\}\), an MLE can converge to the parameter whose model is closest in expected log loss rather than to a literal truth. The estimator may remain useful, but model-based Fisher standard errors can be wrong.

Under suitable conditions, the asymptotic covariance of the square-root-scaled error has the sandwich form

$$
H^{-1}JH^{-1},
$$

where \(H\) is per-observation expected objective curvature and \(J\) is per-observation score variability. The estimator's covariance is therefore approximately \(H^{-1}JH^{-1}/n\). Under a correctly specified regular model, the information identity makes these pieces agree. Under misspecification, they need not.

### Dependence

If observations are clustered or sequential, joint likelihood does not factor into independent row terms. Treating it as though it does often preserves a familiar point estimate while underestimating uncertainty. Cluster-level resampling, cluster-robust calculations, time-series models, or explicit hierarchical likelihoods may be required.

### Selection

Choosing a model, checkpoint, prompt, metric, or stopping time using the same data changes the sampling distribution of the reported estimate. Ordinary fixed-estimator standard errors do not include this selection stage.

**Worked example — best checkpoint.** Suppose 50 checkpoints have identical true quality but noisy validation estimates. Reporting only the maximum validation score produces upward bias. Increasing validation-set size reduces per-checkpoint noise, but the selection bias depends also on the number and dependence of comparisons. An untouched test set estimates the selected checkpoint's performance without reusing the selection noise.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Classify three failures as misspecification, dependence, or selection.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Explain why repeated rows per user may leave a sample mean unchanged but make its iid standard error too small.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a simulation that separates model misspecification from post-selection bias in a many-checkpoint workflow.

## 17. Likelihood and estimation in ML systems

Many familiar ML objectives are likelihood estimators in disguise:

- binary cross-entropy is negative Bernoulli log-likelihood;
- multiclass cross-entropy is negative categorical log-likelihood;
- squared error corresponds to Gaussian conditional likelihood with fixed variance;
- token-level negative log-likelihood fits a conditional categorical distribution at each position.

But several cautions remain:

- a conditional likelihood estimates \(P(Y\mid X)\), not the input distribution \(P(X)\);
- minibatches approximate an optimization objective; they do not create more independent data;
- overparameterized networks can have many parameter values representing the same predictions;
- low training loss does not establish calibration, causal validity, robustness, or task utility;
- token-level likelihood can overweight long documents or correlated sequences;
- evaluation after architecture and hyperparameter search includes selection.

**Worked example — cross-entropy as MLE.** If a classifier emits \(q_\theta(x)\) for \(P(Y=1\mid X=x)\), one observation contributes

$$
y\log q_\theta(x)
+(1-y)\log(1-q_\theta(x)).
$$

Summing this conditional Bernoulli log-likelihood over data and maximizing it is equivalent to minimizing binary cross-entropy. The statistical statement depends on how examples were sampled and whether the conditional model is adequate—not only on whether gradient descent finds a low value.

Before interpreting a fitted number, ask:

1. What population quantity is being estimated?
2. Which randomness defines repeated datasets?
3. Is the model identifiable at the prediction or parameter level?
4. Does the uncertainty calculation include clustering and selection?
5. Would a different loss better match the actual decision?

> **Practice — Foundation:** Match binary cross-entropy, multiclass cross-entropy, and squared error to their basic likelihood models.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the binary cross-entropy objective from a conditional Bernoulli likelihood and identify the iid factorization assumption.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Audit a token-level likelihood comparison between two language models when documents have very different lengths and domains. Propose estimands at both token and document levels.

Run:

python -m labs.checks bernoulli-mle
~~~

The checks cover mixed outcomes, all-zero and all-one boundaries, generators, replication scaling, input preservation, and invalid observations.

### Guided experiment

For true probabilities \(0.02,0.2,0.5,\) and \(0.9\), and several sample sizes:

1. repeat complete Bernoulli datasets many times;
2. plot the sampling distribution of the MLE;
3. measure empirical bias, variance, and MSE;
4. compare empirical standard deviation with the average plug-in standard error;
5. record how often boundary estimates occur;
6. identify where the Gaussian approximation is unreliable.

## 19. Derivations to own

1. Derive the bias–variance decomposition for squared error.
2. Derive bias and variance of an affine transformation of the sample mean.
3. Derive Bernoulli MLE, including boundary cases.
4. Derive Gaussian mean and variance MLEs.
5. Prove the \(n-1\) correction makes sample variance unbiased.
6. Identify sufficient statistics for Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gaussian models.
7. Derive the score and Fisher information for Bernoulli and Gaussian means.
8. Verify the Cramér–Rao bound for a sample mean.
9. Explain MLE consistency through expected log-likelihood and identifiability.

## 20. End-of-unit practice (graded)

**Foundation — problems 1–4.** Distinguish estimation objects and execute direct bias, likelihood, and information calculations.

1. **Language.** For three studies, identify data, target population, estimand, estimator, estimate, and sampling distribution.
2. **Bias and MSE.** Compute bias, variance, and MSE for \(a\bar X+b\) as an estimator of \(\mu\).
3. **Bernoulli likelihood.** Derive and evaluate the likelihood, log-likelihood, score, MLE, and plug-in standard error for 24 successes in 40 trials.
4. **Gaussian estimation.** Compute the Gaussian mean MLE, variance MLE, and unbiased variance estimate for a small dataset.

**Core — problems 5–9.** Derive estimator properties and connect likelihood curvature to uncertainty.

5. **Competing estimators.** Compare the MSE of \(\bar X_n\) and \(a\bar X_n\). Determine the region of \(\mu\) where a specified \(a<1\) improves MSE.
6. **Exponential rate.** Derive the MLE, score, Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, and asymptotic standard error for an iid exponential rate.
7. **Sufficiency.** Factor three likelihoods to identify data summaries sufficient for their parameters; then describe one model change that makes each compression insufficient.
8. **Consistency.** Prove a biased estimator is consistent by separately controlling its bias and variance.
9. **Delta method.** Derive approximate uncertainty for a ratio, log rate, or odds transformation and validate it with repeated simulation.

**Stretch — problems 10–14.** Diagnose nonregularity, misspecification, dependence, and selection in realistic research workflows.

10. **Non-identifiability.** Build a model with a parameter symmetry, show the likelihood has equivalent maxima, and distinguish prediction identifiability from parameter identifiability.
11. **Boundary behavior.** Study Bernoulli MLEs near \(p=0\) at small \(n\). Compare empirical sampling distributions with plug-in Gaussian approximations and explain the zero-standard-error pathology.
12. **Misspecified likelihood.** Fit a single Gaussian to mixture data. Compare model-based Fisher uncertainty, repeated-sample empirical variation, and held-out predictive diagnostics.
13. **Clustered estimation.** Estimate an accuracy difference from prompts nested within users or tasks. Compare row-iid, cluster-aware, and paired uncertainty calculations.
14. **Post-selection estimation.** Simulate selection of the best among many equally good configurations. Quantify validation optimism and test-set correction as the number of candidates and their correlation change.

<details><summary>Worked solution sketches</summary>

1. A complete answer separates the population quantity from its data-dependent rule and treats the sampling distribution as variation across complete repeated datasets, not variation among rows inside one observed dataset.
2. \(E[a\bar X+b]=a\mu+b\), so bias is \((a-1)\mu+b\). Under iid sampling variance is \(a^2\sigma^2/n\); MSE adds the squared bias.
3. With \(s=24,n=40\), \(\hat p=0.6\). The maximized log-likelihood is \(24\log0.6+16\log0.4\), the score vanishes at \(0.6\), and plug-in standard error is \(\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/40}\).
4. The mean is the arithmetic average. Squared deviations divided by \(n\) give the Gaussian variance MLE; dividing by \(n-1\) gives the unbiased estimator.
5. The unshrunk MSE is \(\sigma^2/n\). The shrunk MSE is \(a^2\sigma^2/n+(a-1)^2\mu^2\). Solve the strict inequality between them for the requested \(a\).
6. For exponential density \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), \(\hat\lambda=1/\bar X\), one-observation information is \(1/\lambda^2\), and the asymptotic variance is \(\lambda^2/n\). Verify the parameter is positive and distinguish finite-sample bias from asymptotic behavior.
7. Factorization makes Bernoulli depend on \(\sum X_i\), Poisson on \(\sum X_i\), and Gaussian forms on sums and squared sums depending on which parameters are unknown. Time variation, dependence, or additional parameters can make order or other details informative.
8. One route is Chebyshev around the estimator's expectation: bound stochastic deviation by its vanishing variance, then use the triangle inequality with a deterministic bias that tends to zero.
9. Apply a first-order Taylor expansion. For a ratio, use a two-variable gradient and the full covariance matrix; simulation should resample paired inputs so covariance is preserved.
10. Sign, label-switching, and hidden-unit permutation symmetries all work. Equivalent parameters can produce identical observable laws even when the induced predictive distribution is uniquely determined.
11. Small samples near a boundary frequently produce \(\hat p=0\), whose plug-in standard error is zero. The true repeated-sample error is not zero; the regular interior Taylor approximation has failed.
12. A single Gaussian can target mixture mean and variance while missing modes and tails. Model curvature assumes the fitted family; repeated datasets reveal estimator variation under the mixture; held-out density and residual diagnostics expose predictive misspecification.
13. Row-iid formulas omit within-cluster covariance. Cluster-aware methods use independent clusters; pairing uses within-unit differences. The correct comparison depends on the intended population of new prompts, users, or tasks.
14. Maximizing noisy validation values creates optimism. An untouched test set removes reuse of validation noise for the selected model, while more candidates generally increase optimism and stronger correlation among candidates reduces the effective number of distinct comparisons.

</details>

## Mastery check

Given an unfamiliar estimation problem, name the target and sampling unit; propose an estimator; derive or simulate its bias, variance, and MSE; write and maximize a likelihood; check boundaries and identifiability; calculate information and an asymptotic standard error when regularity permits; and explain how misspecification, dependence, regularization, or selection changes the conclusion.
